entry.title: How the VM Actually Executes a Program in SQLite
entry.summary: Hello, I'm Maneshwar. I'm working on git-lrc: a Git hook for Checking AI generated code. So far, we’ve looked at bytecode instructions, insert logic, and join logic. But we haven’t yet stepped into the interpreter itself. Today we answer a very direct question: How does SQLite’s VM execute a bytecode program? Every bytecode program starts at instruction 0. The VM continues executing instructions until one of three things happens: It encounters an explicit Halt instruction. The program counter (pc) moves past the last instruction this is treated as an implicit Halt. An execution error occurs. When execution stops, SQLite performs cleanup, all open cursors are closed, memory allocated to the VM is released and if an error occurred, any pending transaction is rolled back. UUIDs are everywhere — database primary keys, distributed systems, API request tracing. But with UUID v7 now standardized in RFC 9562, the landscape has changed. Here's what you need to know.
Version Based On Sortable When to Use
v1 Timestamp + MAC Partially Legacy systems
v4 Random No General purpose (most common)
v5 SHA-1 hash No Deterministic IDs from names
v7 Timestamp + Random Yes New projects (recommended)

entry.title: What Being a Founding Engineer Actually Means (Beyond Writing Code)
entry.summary: Most people think a founding engineer writes code. That’s maybe 30% of the job. The rest is ambiguity, architectural responsibility, and making decisions that shape a product long before scale is visible. In early-stage environments, there is no predefined system. You are the system. You don’t inherit decisions. You make them: Database structure Auth model API design Deployment strategy What to build now vs later What to deliberately avoid Every shortcut becomes future technical debt. You operate in that tension daily. Early-stage products evolve fast. Features pivot. If the foundation is tightly coupled, iteration becomes expensive. So you think ahead: Where will this break? What will scale? What must remain flexible? You optimize for adaptability — not perfection. There’s no clear roadmap. You don’t know: What user growth will look like What features will dominate usage Which integrations will matter most Yet you still have to choose: Simple now vs scalable later Speed vs structure Abstraction vs clarity There’s no formula. Only judgment. If something breaks, it’s your system. If performance degrades, it’s your data model. If deployment fails, it’s your infra decision. You can’t hide behind “that’s not my module.” A founding engineer doesn’t just ship code. They carry architectural responsibility. The difference isn’t seniority. It’s perspective. You stop thinking: “How do I implement this feature?” And start thinking: “How does this decision affect the system 6 months from now?” That shift changes how you design everything. Early products don’t fail because of missing features. They fail because the foundation can’t support growth. Being a founding engineer means designing that foundation — under uncertainty. This is just a high-level view. The detailed breakdown of how I design and ship backend systems is here: You can see more of my work and writing here → https://www.vishwamdhavale.com
